title: Function Factory
tagline: You build a machine (a function) once, then use it again and again.
objectives: Say why one machine (a function) beats the same lines copied many times.
Write a function with a slot (a parameter) that hands something back (return).
Use the same function many times, with a different order each time.

config.headline: Today you build a machine once and use it again and again.
lines: The Studio's box office has twelve orders on the counter. Every order needs the same two things. One is a label with the name and the number of seats on it. The other is the cost. Until today, a program that did that job had two lines typed out for every order, and those two lines looked nearly the same every time.

Here is what that program looks like, just below. It works. It is also very long. The same two lines come round for every order, with only the name and the numbers changed, so if those lines are wrong, they are wrong in twelve places.

A factory does not build a new machine for every order. It builds the machine once, and then feeds every order through it. Today you build machines like that. In Python, a machine like this is called a FUNCTION.
A function has a name, a slot for what goes in, and a way of handing the finished thing back out. You write it once. Then you can use it as many times as you like, with a different order each time.
Here is what happens in the next hour, in the order it happens.
1. First you watch a short film. It has no sound.

2. Then you do three training builds. In the first you read a machine that is already built, and fix one word in it. In the second you put the lines of a machine in the right order. In the third you fill in the gaps in a machine.
3. Then you build your own factory. It has two machines, and the factory floor feeds twelve orders through them.

4. Then comes the Rush. You are paired with somebody in this room, at another computer. They send you three orders, your machines make the products, and they check what came out. You do the same for them.
You are not told who your partner is until the end. You each get a call sign instead — a made-up name, like Foreman 4. They see your call sign, and you see theirs.
5. After the Rush there is a screen with four small extra jobs on it. They are there if you want them, and none of them is marked.
The hour ends with one marked question and the How did it go? screen.

config.shapeTitle: Build it once, use it many times
config.shapeLead: Every machine in this lesson has the same shape. First comes a def line with the machine's name and its slot (or its two slots). Then comes one line pushed in under it, which hands the product back with return. After that you can use the machine as many times as you like.
config.title: Build your factory
config.intro: This is the factory you build yourself. It has two machines, and both must do what the spec card says. The floor feeds twelve orders through them. The film shows how to read the spec card, and what the reject bin tells you.
config.introVideoSay: This film is three minutes long. It shows how to read the spec card, and what the reject bin tells you.
config.emptySay: Your factory is empty. Type the two machines, or press Put the shape in for me.
config.starterSay: Want the shape put in for you? Both machines will still be empty inside. The two lines at the bottom use the machines. You can change those two lines if you like.
config.starterLabel: Put the shape in for me
config.starterDoneSay: The shape is in. Now write the inside of each machine — the return line — and press RUN.

floor.title: The factory floor
floor.lead: The floor drops every order into your machine and shows what comes out.
floor.wrongStamp: not what the spec asked for
floor.rejectLead: These products came out wrong. Each one is shown beside what it should be.
floor.noMachine: The floor cannot find a machine called {fn}. Check the name on your def line.
floor.allNoneSay: Every product came back as None — {stamp}. The machine printed instead of handing back with return. One is shown beside what it should be:

spec.title: The spec card
spec.lead: Every order on the floor is a name and a number of seats. Your factory needs these two machines:

rows.gives: the name, a space, the letter x, a space, then the seats
the seats times 4 — a seat is 4 pounds

spec.note: The label machine has TWO slots, with a comma between them. str( ) wraps a number so a + can join it onto words.

builds.planLabel: The two machines your factory needs
builds.goalLine: Build two machines: label, which makes the label for an order, and cost, which works out what it costs.
builds.brief: Read the spec card. Then build both machines in the box, and use each one once at the bottom so you can see it work. When you press RUN, the floor drops all twelve orders into your machines.

features.reference:
def label(name, seats):
    return name + " x " + str(seats)
features.label: label makes the right label for every order.
features.nudge: Look at the reject bin: it shows your label beside the label the spec wanted. Check the spaces and the x, and check str( ) is wrapping the seats.

features.label: cost works out the right cost for every order.
features.nudge: Look at the reject bin. If the stamp on a cost says nothing came back, your machine printed instead of using return. If a cost is the wrong number, the inside is not the seats times 4.

builds.shapeNote: Build every machine before you use it. The line pushed in under def is the machine's inside, and return is how it hands the product back.
builds.matchedSay: Twelve orders went in. Twelve labels and twelve costs came out, and every one is correct. All of them came from two machines you wrote once. That is what a function is for: you write it once, and you use it again and again.
builds.notYetSay: Your factory is not making every product yet. The reject bin shows each wrong product beside the one the spec wanted. Fix one machine at a time, then press RUN again.

builds.offerKicker: Here is one more thing to try, if you want it.
builds.offerLead: There is a third machine you can build. It USES your first two: it calls label and cost, and hands back one line with both in it. It is not worth any points, and you can skip it.
builds.offerFree: You get no points either way.
builds.goalLine: Build receipt(name, seats): it hands back the label, a space, a dash, a space, the cost, a space, and the word pounds — like Aoife x 2 - 8 pounds.
builds.brief: Your two machines are already in the box. A machine can use another machine: inside receipt, write label(name, seats) and cost(seats) where you need them. The cost is a number, so str( ) has to wrap it before a + can join it onto words.

features.label: receipt hands back the label and the cost in one line, for every order.
features.nudge: Look at the reject bin. Check the dash has a space on each side, check str( ) is wrapping cost(seats), and check the word pounds is at the end.

builds.shapeNote: This is a machine calling a machine. label and cost each hand something back, and receipt joins the two together.
builds.matchedSay: Your receipt machine uses two other machines. Big programs are built the same way: people write small machines that each do one job, and then join them together.
builds.notYetSay: The receipt machine is not working yet. Read the reject bin: it shows your receipt beside the one the spec wanted.
builds.finishLabel: Finish this part and carry on

config.help:
1. Read the spec card. It asks for two machines.
2. Watch the short film.
3. Press Start building.
4. Type both machines into the box called Your factory, or press Put the shape in for me and then write the inside of each machine.
5. Press RUN my program. The floor drops twelve orders into your machines and shows a product card for each. Anything wrong goes in the reject bin, beside the product the spec wanted.
6. When the card says BOTH MACHINES WORK, press Continue.

config.title: The Rush: partner orders
config.intro: Your factory works. Now somebody else in this room sends it orders. You are paired with a classmate at another computer. They write three orders, your machines make the products, and they check what came out. You do the same for them.
steps: You are given a **call sign** — a made-up name like Foreman 4. That is the only name your partner sees, and theirs is the only name you see.
You write three orders: a name and a number of seats each.
Your orders go to their factory, and theirs come to yours. Your machines make the products.
You check the products that came back from their factory: is each one what you ordered?

sideShow.name: Unit 7
sideShow.alt: Unit 7, a cartoon factory robot with a dented chest plate and one drooping antenna
sideShow.open: Unit 7 reporting. I have made this same part four thousand and twelve times. By hand. This one is slightly worse than the last one.
lines: Nobody has asked me for a part in nearly a minute. I do not know what to do with my arms.
I once tried to make two parts at the same time. We do not talk about it.
The conveyor belt and I are not speaking. It knows what it did.
I have a dream. In the dream, somebody builds a machine, and I sit down.
Four thousand and thirteen. I have started another one. I could not help myself.
If you are still waiting, so am I. We are waiting together. This is the nicest thing that has happened to me all week.
sideShow.exitLine: A PARTNER! ORDERS! A REASON TO EXIST! Please excuse the shouting — go, go, they are waiting!
sideShow.leaveLine: Off you go. I will be here, making part four thousand and fourteen.

config.help:
The Rush has four parts.

1. You are paired with a classmate, and you both get a call sign.
2. You write three orders — a name and a number of seats each — and press Send my orders.
3. Their orders arrive. Press RUN and your factory makes the products, which go back to them.
4. Their products arrive. For each one, click Yes or No: is it what you ordered?

If nobody is free to pair with you, the Studio sends you three orders instead, and you check the products yourself. Press the button at the bottom to leave the Rush and carry on with the lesson.

builds.title: Job 1 — the slots the other way round
builds.whiff: See what happens when the name and the seats go into the wrong slots.
builds.goalLine: Run this program and read what comes out. Then swap the name and the number of seats back the right way round.
builds.brief: A machine fills its slots in order. The first thing in the brackets goes into the first slot, and the second thing goes into the second slot. Put them the wrong way round, and the machine does not check what you gave it. The number goes into the slot meant for a name, and the name goes into the slot meant for the seats.

blanks.label: the name and the number of seats — the first one goes into the first slot

example.lead: Try it as it is first. The first label comes out fine. Then Python stops at the last line, because the number 2 went into the slot meant for a name, and a number cannot be joined onto words. Read what it says. Then change the last line so the name and the seats are in the right slots.
example.after: This job shows one thing. A machine takes whatever is dropped into its slots, in order. It does not check what you gave it.

builds.matchedSay: It runs all the way through now: the name goes in first and the seats second, and both labels come out right.
builds.notYetSay: Python stopped at the last line. That is what this job is about. Read what Python said in the console. Then put the name and the seats in the right slots, and press RUN again.
builds.runCheckedSay: This job is about reading what comes out, so this card does not check what your program printed. Press RUN, read the console, then fix the last line.

builds.title: Job 2 — the list of names
builds.whiff: A loop feeds every name in a list through your machine.
builds.goalLine: Feed every name in a list through the label machine, one after another.
builds.brief: You met a loop in Lesson 3. A loop goes through a list one thing at a time. Here, the loop drops each name into the label machine.
builds.matchedSay: One machine and one loop made four labels. If the list had a fifth name, the loop would make a fifth label, and nothing else would have to change.

builds.title: Job 3 — the named slot
builds.whiff: Fill a slot by its name, so the order inside the brackets stops mattering.
builds.goalLine: Use the machine by naming its slots, in either order.
builds.brief: You can fill a slot by writing its name and an = sign inside the brackets. Then the order does not matter, because each thing goes to the slot you named.
builds.matchedSay: Both labels are right, even though the second line named the slots the other way round.

builds.title: Job 4 — the slot with a usual value
builds.whiff: A slot can have a usual value built in. It uses that value unless you give it a different one.
builds.goalLine: Give the cost machine a price slot that is usually 4. Then use the machine twice: once without a price, and once with a different price in the brackets.
builds.brief: A slot can carry its usual value in the def line, like price=4. Leave that slot empty when you use the machine and it uses 4. Give it a number and it uses yours.
builds.matchedSay: The first use printed 8, with the usual price. The second use printed 20, because the brackets gave it a different price, 10. That is one machine used in two ways.
